title: Does Alcohol Lower Testosterone? What the Research Says (and TRT)
excerpt: Does alcohol lower testosterone? How drinking affects male hormones by amount, how fast levels recover, what it means for lifters, and drinking safely on TRT.
metaDescription: Does alcohol lower testosterone? How much drinking it takes, how long the drop lasts, beer vs spirits, recovery after cutting back, and alcohol on TRT.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, alcohol can lower testosterone, but how much depends almost entirely on how much you drink. A drink or two with dinner has little measurable effect in most men. A heavy night out pushes testosterone down for roughly the next day. Drinking heavily most days, over months and years, is a well-established cause of genuinely low testosterone, along with shrunken testicles, lower sex drive, erection problems, and in some men, breast tissue growth. The good news is that in most men who cut back before serious liver damage sets in, levels tend to recover.

**The quick rules:** If you care about your testosterone, keep drinking occasional and moderate, avoid binge sessions (around five or more drinks in one sitting for men), protect your sleep on nights you drink, and don't drink right after hard training. If you're on testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), there's no known dangerous direct interaction with an occasional drink, but heavy drinking works against what the treatment is trying to do and adds to several of its side effects. Tell your prescriber what you actually drink.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on alcohol and hormones. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your history. **See a doctor if** you have ongoing low sex drive, erection problems, unexplained fatigue, loss of muscle, low mood, breast swelling or tenderness, or shrinking testicles; if you're on TRT and drink more than a few drinks a week; or if you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or swelling in your belly or legs, which can be signs of liver trouble. If you're considering starting, stopping, or changing any hormone treatment, talk to your doctor first.

## How Alcohol Lowers Testosterone: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Testosterone in men is made mostly in the testicles, in cells called Leydig cells. They don't work on their own. They take orders from a chain of command that starts in the brain: the hypothalamus releases a signal hormone, which tells the pituitary gland to release luteinizing hormone (LH), which travels in the blood and tells the Leydig cells to make testosterone. Doctors call this chain the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, or HPG axis. Alcohol interferes at several points along it.

### 1. It slows the factory directly

When your liver and other tissues break down alcohol, the chemistry shifts the balance of a helper molecule called NAD+ toward its "used" form, NADH. Making testosterone relies on enzymes that need that same helper molecule. With too much of it tied up processing alcohol, the testosterone-making steps in the Leydig cells slow down. Alcohol and its first breakdown product, acetaldehyde, are also directly toxic to these cells at high, repeated exposure. This is the main reason testosterone dips after a heavy night, and it's a big part of why long-term heavy drinkers can end up with smaller testicles.

### 2. It muffles the signal from the brain

Heavy drinking blunts the release of the signal hormones from the hypothalamus and pituitary. In a healthy system, a drop in testosterone would trigger the brain to send a stronger LH signal to compensate. Alcohol can interfere with that correction, so levels stay down instead of bouncing back.

### 3. It turns more testosterone into estrogen

Men need some estrogen, and they make it by converting testosterone with an enzyme called aromatase. Alcohol increases aromatase activity, and fat tissue, especially belly fat, is full of aromatase. A damaged liver also clears estrogen less effectively. Put those together over years of heavy drinking and the hormone balance shifts: less testosterone, more estrogen. That's why breast tissue growth (gynecomastia) is a classic sign in men with advanced alcohol-related liver disease.

### 4. It raises the protein that locks testosterone up

Most testosterone in your blood is bound to a carrier protein called sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG). Bound testosterone isn't available to your tissues; the "free" portion is what does the work. Long-term heavy drinking and liver disease tend to raise SHBG, so even when total testosterone looks okay on paper, the usable fraction can be lower. This is one reason doctors sometimes check free testosterone, not just the total.

### 5. It wrecks the sleep testosterone depends on

A large share of the day's testosterone release happens during sleep, and morning levels are highest for a reason. Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep. A widely cited 2011 study in *JAMA* (Leproult and Van Cauter) found that healthy young men restricted to about five hours of sleep a night for one week had daytime testosterone roughly 10 to 15 percent lower than when well rested. Alcohol doesn't cause that much sleep loss on a single night, but repeated poor sleep after drinking adds up. If drinking keeps you awake at 3 a.m., our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on.

### 6. It raises stress hormones

Heavy drinking and the withdrawal-like rebound the next morning raise cortisol, the body's main stress hormone. Cortisol and testosterone tend to move in opposite directions, and chronically high cortisol is associated with lower testosterone.

## What the Research Actually Shows, by Amount

The single most useful idea on this page is that the effect is dose-dependent. Here's how the research breaks down in practical terms.

### One or two drinks

Studies of light to moderate drinking in healthy men generally find either no meaningful change in testosterone or a small, short-lived dip. A controlled Dutch trial in the early 2000s gave healthy middle-aged men a moderate amount of alcohol every evening (roughly three drinks) for three weeks and compared it with three weeks without alcohol. Testosterone came out a few percent lower on the alcohol weeks. That's real but small, well within the normal day-to-day swings of testosterone, and not something you would feel.

Some studies have even found a brief rise in testosterone shortly after a small dose, particularly in women. The likely explanation is that the liver's processing of alcohol temporarily slows the breakdown of hormones. It is short-lived and not a reason to drink.

### A heavy night out

This is where effects become clear. After an evening of heavy drinking, studies consistently find that testosterone drops over the following hours and is often noticeably lower the next day, with recovery typically within a day or two. The drop is driven by the direct effect on the Leydig cells plus a bad night's sleep. A single episode is unlikely to cause lasting harm, but it's not nothing if it's happening every weekend.

### Heavy drinking most days, for years

This is the category where alcohol is a recognized medical cause of low testosterone (hypogonadism). Long-term heavy drinkers are more likely to have low testosterone, low sperm counts and poorer sperm quality, smaller testicles, reduced sex drive, and erectile dysfunction. Men who go on to develop cirrhosis often show the full picture, including gynecomastia, loss of body hair, and testicular atrophy. These changes come from the combination of direct testicular damage, disrupted brain signaling, extra estrogen, and liver disease. If you're thinking about having children, our [guide to alcohol and fertility](/never-hungover/alcohol-fertility-reproductive-health-guide-2025) covers the sperm side of this in more detail.

### The honest caveat

Not every observational study finds a straight line. Some large population studies report little difference in testosterone between moderate drinkers and non-drinkers. That's partly because many things affect testosterone at once (age, body fat, sleep, illness, other medicines) and partly because people who don't drink at all include some who stopped for health reasons. The controlled studies and the clinical evidence from heavy drinkers are clearer: more alcohol means more suppression.

## Does the Type of Drink Matter? (Beer, Wine, and Spirits)

The question "does beer lower testosterone" comes up a lot, usually because of hops. Hops contain plant compounds that weakly mimic estrogen, the strongest of which is called 8-prenylnaringenin. In concentrated extracts, these compounds have measurable effects. In beer, the amounts are small, and you'd run into the problems of the alcohol itself long before the hop compounds became meaningful.

In practice, the alcohol is what matters, not the source. Ten beers and the equivalent amount of whiskey will both suppress testosterone. Wine has no special protection either; red wine's antioxidants don't offset the alcohol.

What beer does have is calories. Regular heavy beer drinking tends to add belly fat, and belly fat is a major site of testosterone-to-estrogen conversion. So the "beer belly" itself contributes more to lower testosterone than anything specific in the beer. Our guide on [alcohol and weight loss](/never-hungover/alcohol-weight-loss-metabolic-guide-2025) covers how drinking affects body fat.

## Alcohol, Testosterone, and the Gym

If you lift or train hard, alcohol's effect on hormones is one piece of a bigger recovery story. Researchers have looked at drinking after resistance training. The results on testosterone itself are mixed, with some small studies finding little change. The clearer finding comes from work on muscle repair: a study from Australian researchers (Parr and colleagues, 2014) found that a large dose of alcohol after hard exercise reduced muscle protein synthesis, the process of rebuilding muscle, even when protein was eaten alongside it.

In other words, if your goal is building muscle, a heavy session right after training hurts you through several routes at once: hormone dips, poor sleep, slower muscle repair, and lost training quality the next day. Our breakdown of [alcohol and muscle protein synthesis](/never-hungover/alcohol-protein-synthesis-muscle-recovery-impact-guide-2025) goes deeper, and our [guide for fitness-minded social drinkers](/never-hungover/fitness-enthusiast-social-drinking-dhm-2025) has practical strategies.

Practical tips for lifters who drink:

- **Separate training and drinking.** Avoid drinking heavily on the same evening as a hard session, when your body is in repair mode.
- **Eat protein first.** It doesn't fully offset alcohol, but it helps.
- **Keep it moderate.** Most of the damage in the research comes from large doses, not a beer or two.
- **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed and drink water alongside alcohol.

## Signs Your Drinking Might Be Affecting Your Testosterone

Low testosterone has vague symptoms that overlap with plenty of other problems, including simply drinking too much. Common signs include:

- Lower sex drive than you're used to
- Erection problems, or fewer morning erections
- Persistent tiredness that sleep doesn't fix
- Low mood, irritability, or poor concentration
- Losing muscle or strength despite training
- Gaining belly fat
- Breast tenderness or swelling
- Testicles that seem smaller or softer

Note that alcohol can cause several of these directly, whatever your testosterone level. "Whiskey dick," the temporary erection trouble after heavy drinking, is mostly about alcohol depressing the nervous system and blood flow in the moment, not testosterone. Likewise, tiredness and low mood after drinking are often just the after-effects of alcohol and poor sleep.

### Getting it checked properly

If you have symptoms, the right move is a blood test through a doctor, not guessing or buying a home kit and reading too much into it. Testosterone peaks in the morning and varies day to day, so clinical guidelines, including those from the Endocrine Society, recommend measuring it with a morning blood draw and confirming a low result with a second test on a different day before diagnosing low testosterone.

Practical tips for an accurate test:

- Book it for the morning, ideally before 10 a.m.
- Avoid heavy drinking for at least a couple of days beforehand, so you're not measuring a temporary dip.
- Get a normal night's sleep before the test.
- Tell your doctor honestly how much you drink. It changes how they interpret the result and what they recommend.

## Alcohol and TRT: What to Know If You're on Testosterone Therapy

If you're on testosterone replacement therapy (injections, gels, patches, or pellets), you might wonder whether you can still drink. **Talk to your doctor about your own situation, since they know your dose, your blood work, and your other medicines.** Here's the general picture.

### Is there a direct interaction?

There's no well-known, direct chemical interaction between testosterone therapy and alcohol of the kind you'd see with, for example, sedatives or certain antibiotics. An occasional drink is generally not considered a problem for most men on TRT. The concerns come from side effects the two have in common, which add up when drinking is heavy.

### Where alcohol and TRT overlap

- **Undermining the treatment.** Heavy drinking works against TRT by suppressing your own remaining production, raising SHBG, and increasing the conversion of testosterone to estrogen. Some men on TRT who drink heavily notice more estrogen-type side effects, such as breast tenderness or water retention.
- **Red blood cell count.** TRT commonly raises hematocrit, the proportion of your blood made up of red cells, and doctors monitor it because blood that's too thick raises clot risk. Alcohol doesn't cause that, but being dehydrated after drinking can make a blood test read higher than your true level. Hydrate well and avoid drinking heavily before your blood work.
- **Blood pressure.** Regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure, and TRT can raise it in some men. The two together deserve monitoring.
- **Sleep apnea.** TRT can worsen untreated obstructive sleep apnea, and this is a standard caution on testosterone products. Alcohol relaxes the throat muscles and makes snoring and apnea worse. If you snore heavily or wake up gasping, mention it to your doctor.
- **The liver.** Most modern TRT (injections, gels, patches) is not hard on the liver. Older oral forms of testosterone carried liver risks, and anabolic steroids used outside medical care can seriously damage the liver. If you're taking any oral hormone or unprescribed product and drinking heavily, that combination deserves real caution and a conversation with a doctor.
- **Mood.** Both alcohol and changes in hormone levels can affect mood and irritability. If you notice mood swings, tell your prescriber.

### A sensible approach on TRT

Keep drinking moderate, hydrate, don't drink heavily before blood tests, and be honest with your prescriber about your intake. If you're using testosterone without a prescription or medical monitoring, alcohol is the smaller problem; see a doctor so your blood counts, blood pressure, and liver can be checked.

## Can Your Testosterone Recover After Cutting Back?

For most men, yes. Studies following heavy drinkers who stop or sharply reduce their intake generally show testosterone and related hormones improving over the following weeks to months. The more advanced the damage, particularly with cirrhosis or significant testicular atrophy, the less complete the recovery tends to be.

Cutting back also helps indirectly: you sleep better, tend to lose belly fat, and recover from training more effectively. Those changes support healthy testosterone on their own.

If you're a light or moderate drinker, quitting entirely is unlikely to make a dramatic difference to your testosterone. The bigger levers for most men are:

1. **Sleep.** Seven to nine hours of decent sleep is one of the strongest everyday factors.
2. **Body fat.** Losing excess belly fat reduces testosterone-to-estrogen conversion.
3. **Resistance training.** Regular strength training supports healthy hormone levels and body composition.
4. **Avoiding binges.** Spreading the same drinks out across the week is less disruptive than packing them into one night, though less overall is better still.

A note for anyone who drinks every day and finds it hard to cut back: if you get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or nauseous when you go without, or you've ever had a seizure or hallucinations after stopping, don't quit suddenly on your own. Stopping abruptly after heavy daily drinking can be dangerous. Talk to a doctor, who can help you cut back safely.

## What About Women?

Alcohol affects hormones in women too, but differently. Studies have found that alcohol can briefly raise testosterone in women, and long-term drinking is linked to higher estrogen levels, which is one of the reasons heavy drinking is associated with a higher risk of breast cancer. If you're a woman searching this topic because of hormone symptoms, irregular periods, or perimenopause, it's worth a conversation with your doctor, who can look at the full picture.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Let's be clear: **there is no good evidence that DHM, or any hangover supplement, protects your testosterone from alcohol.** No supplement offsets the hormonal effects of heavy drinking. What actually protects testosterone from alcohol is drinking less, sleeping well, and staying fit.

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound studied mainly for how the body processes alcohol and for hangover symptoms. Most of the research is from animal studies, with limited human data. Some people find it helps them feel better the morning after a night out, which may make it easier to stick to your training and sleep routine. That's a reasonable, modest expectation. It's not a hormone treatment.

If you want to try it, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) compares the options for overall liver support. For the habits with the strongest evidence, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- **Light drinking** (a drink or two, not every day) has little measurable effect on testosterone for most men.
- **Heavy nights** cause a temporary drop that usually recovers within a day or two.
- **Heavy drinking most days** is a well-established cause of low testosterone, low fertility, erection problems, and more estrogen-type effects, especially once the liver is involved.
- **The type of drink doesn't matter** much; total alcohol, sleep, and belly fat do.
- **On TRT**, an occasional drink is generally fine, but heavy drinking undermines the treatment and adds to its side effects. Tell your prescriber what you drink.
- **If you have symptoms**, get two morning blood tests through a doctor before drawing conclusions.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol lower testosterone?**

Heavy drinking does, and regular heavy drinking can lower it for the long term. A night of heavy drinking typically pushes testosterone down for roughly the next day, and years of heavy drinking are a well-known cause of low testosterone, shrunken testicles, and breast tissue growth in men. Light to moderate drinking has a much smaller effect: controlled studies find either no meaningful change or a small dip of a few percent.

**How much alcohol lowers testosterone?**

There is no single cutoff that applies to everyone. The research pattern is that one or two drinks has little measurable effect, binge-level drinking (roughly five or more drinks in a session for men) causes a temporary drop, and drinking heavily most days is where lasting suppression shows up. Your sleep, body fat, age, and liver health all change how much it matters for you.

**How long does alcohol lower testosterone for?**

After a single heavy session, levels usually come back toward normal within about a day or two, once the alcohol is cleared and you've slept properly. After long-term heavy drinking, recovery takes longer. Studies of men who stop drinking show testosterone often improves over weeks to months, as long as the liver and testicles haven't been seriously damaged.

**Can I drink alcohol while on TRT?**

There's no known direct, dangerous chemical interaction between testosterone therapy and an occasional drink, and many men on TRT drink in moderation. The problems are overlapping side effects: heavy drinking can raise blood pressure, worsen sleep apnea, add strain to the liver, raise estrogen through more conversion of testosterone, and leave you dehydrated before blood tests, which can make your red blood cell count look higher. Tell your prescriber how much you actually drink and follow their advice.

**Does beer lower testosterone more than other drinks?**

Not in any way that matters at normal intake. Hops contain plant compounds that act like weak estrogens, but the amounts in beer are tiny compared with the effect of the alcohol itself. What matters is the total amount of alcohol you drink, not whether it comes from beer, wine, or spirits. A beer belly matters more than the beer, because extra belly fat converts testosterone into estrogen.

**Will quitting alcohol raise my testosterone?**

If you drink heavily, cutting back or stopping is one of the more reliable ways to help your levels recover, especially when it also improves your sleep and helps you lose belly fat. If you only drink lightly, quitting is unlikely to change your testosterone much. If you have symptoms of low testosterone, get two morning blood tests through a doctor rather than guessing.

**Does alcohol increase estrogen in men?**

Heavy, long-term drinking can. Alcohol increases the activity of aromatase, the enzyme that turns testosterone into estrogen, and liver damage reduces how well the body clears estrogen. That is why men with advanced alcohol-related liver disease often develop breast tissue growth. Occasional moderate drinking is unlikely to produce a noticeable shift.

**Does DHM help protect testosterone from alcohol?**

There is no good evidence that DHM protects testosterone or hormone levels. DHM is studied for how the body handles alcohol and for hangover symptoms, mostly in animals and small human studies. If your goal is protecting testosterone, the things that work are drinking less, sleeping well, keeping body fat down, and lifting weights.
